courses.title: Theories of International Relations
courses.description: A systematic introduction to the competing theoretical traditions that structure the study of world politics, from realism and liberalism to constructivism and critical approaches, tested against historical cases.
objectives: Compare realism, liberalism and constructivism on the same empirical puzzles
Apply levels of analysis to explain foreign policy decisions
Evaluate theory against evidence from historical cases
Write a theoretically grounded analytical essay

modules.i: Sovereignty and the absence of world government set the background conditions for all international politics.
o: Explain how anarchy structures state behaviour
Identify institutions of the state system
r: Waltz, Theory of International Politics, ch. 5
modules.a: Write 300 words on which international institutions constrain states most, using one historical example.
modules.l: Anarchy in IR is a structural claim, not a description of chaos: no authority stands above states. Realists derive self-help from that premise, liberals the demand for institutions, and constructivists ask how the meaning of anarchy is produced in practice.

modules.i: Realism explains state behaviour through the distribution of power and the permanent risk of conflict.
r: Mearsheimer, The Tragedy of Great Power Politics, ch. 2
modules.a: Identify one policy decision that fits realist expectations and one that contradicts them.
modules.l: Structural realism locates the cause of state behaviour in the distribution of capabilities rather than in human nature. The security dilemma follows: defensive measures by one state read as threats to another, so cooperation becomes precarious even when all parties prefer peace.

modules.i: Liberal theory asks when institutions, trade and domestic politics make cooperation durable.
r: Doyle, 'Kant, Liberal Legacies and Foreign Affairs'
modules.a: Test the democratic peace claim against two dyads of your choice and record the result.
modules.l: Liberals argue that repetition, information and issue linkage let states escape the worst of anarchy. The mechanism is not goodwill but calculated reciprocity: institutions raise the cost of defection and lengthen the shadow of the future.

modules.i: Constructivism holds that interests are not given but produced by identities and norms.
o: Trace norm diffusion in one case
r: Wendt, 'Anarchy is What States Make of It'
modules.a: Trace how the norm against anti-personnel landmines spread, noting the actors involved.
modules.l: For constructivists the structure of international politics is social as well as material. If states understand themselves as rivals or as partners, the same capabilities produce different behaviour, which makes identity and legitimacy central variables rather than decoration.

modules.i: Explanations shift depending on whether we look at individuals, states or the international system.
o: Apply the three standard levels of analysis
Show how level choice changes explanation
modules.a: Explain one crisis at each level and compare the resulting accounts.
modules.l: Level of analysis is a methodological choice with substantive consequences. Systemic accounts explain recurring patterns but not timing; state-level accounts explain policy but not system change; individual accounts explain decisions but struggle to generalise.

modules.i: Alliances are the visible instrument through which balancing occurs.
r: Walt, The Origins of Alliances, ch. 1
modules.a: Model an alliance decision during a regional crisis and justify the expected choice.
modules.l: Alliances aggregate capability but create two risks: entrapment in a partner's quarrel and abandonment if the partner loses interest. Credibility is therefore the currency of alliance politics, and it is built through visible commitments rather than declarations.

modules.i: Foreign policy is made by governments whose choices are shaped by coalitions, bureaucracies and publics.
r: Allison and Zelikow, Essence of Decision, ch. 3
modules.a: Analyse a treaty negotiation as a two-level game with separate win-sets.
modules.l: Putnam's two-level game shows that international agreements must be ratified domestically, so negotiators bargain simultaneously at both tables. What looks like weakness abroad is often a genuine constraint at home, and skilled negotiators use it deliberately.

modules.i: The final module asks students to defend one theoretical account against rivals using evidence.
o: Select and justify a theoretical framework
r: George and Bennett, Case Studies and Theory Development, ch. 1
Sample essay in the course reader
modules.a: Submit the course essay plan: question, theory, case and evidence sources.
modules.l: Theory choice should follow the puzzle rather than habit. If the question concerns why a decision was taken, process tracing carries the burden; if it concerns why outcomes recur, comparison across cases is stronger than a single narrative.

courses.title: Eurasia and the Post-Soviet Space
courses.description: An advanced regional studies course on the politics, security and political economy of the post-Soviet space, from the Soviet legacy and contested borders to energy geopolitics and regional organisations.
objectives: Analyse how Soviet institutional legacies shape contemporary statehood
Explain the security dynamics of unresolved conflicts
Assess the role of energy and sanctions in regional politics
Produce a research-based country or thematic study

modules.i: Post-Soviet states inherited both institutions and unresolved questions of nationhood.
o: Identify institutional legacies of the USSR
r: Suny, The Revenge of the Past, ch. 2
modules.a: Compare two states' language laws and explain the political logic of each.
modules.l: The Soviet system organised territory around nationality while suppressing nationalism's political expression. When that constraint lifted, both the federal structure and the nationality categories became resources for new states and claims against them.

modules.i: Administrative borders drawn for a different polity became international frontiers overnight.
o: Apply uti possidetis to the region
r: King, The Ghost of Freedom, ch. 4
modules.a: Map one contested territory and list the legal and political claims of each party.
modules.l: Borders in the region combine Soviet-era cartography with post-1991 recognition politics. Because internal administrative lines were never designed as international borders, delimitation disputes easily acquire symbolic and security dimensions.

modules.i: Pipeline routes and pricing disputes make energy a core instrument of regional influence.
o: Explain pricing disputes as political events
modules.a: Draw the main export routes from the Caspian and note which actor controls each segment.
modules.l: Energy infrastructure is political because routes are few, costly and long-lived. Control over transit gives leverage, but dependence cuts both ways: producers need buyers, and states that rely on a single corridor remain exposed to the transit state.

modules.i: Protracted conflicts shape the security architecture of the region.
o: Assess the effect of conflict on regional order
r: Lynch, Engaging Eurasia's Separatist States, ch. 1
modules.a: Compare two mediation formats and argue which produced the more durable outcome.
modules.l: Unresolved conflicts endure because the parties prefer an unsettled status quo to a costly settlement, and external patrons have no incentive to force one. Negotiation formats then become instruments of position-holding rather than of resolution.

modules.i: Overlapping organisations compete for members, mandates and legitimacy.
o: Assess economic integration in the EAEU
modules.a: Build a comparison table of the three organisations across mandate, membership and enforcement.
modules.l: Post-Soviet organisations do not replicate the EU model. They are typically lighter in enforcement and broader in declared scope, which lets members join several at once and makes overlap a political instrument rather than an anomaly.

modules.t: Europe, Enlargement and the Eastern Partnership
modules.i: EU instruments reshape the incentives of neighbouring states without offering membership guarantees.
r: Course notes on Eastern Partnership instruments
modules.a: Compare the obligations in two association agreements and rank their domestic cost.
modules.l: EU conditionality works through regulatory approximation rather than enforcement. Neighbours adopt rules to gain market access, but the adjustments are costly and unevenly distributed, which is why domestic coalitions matter as much as Brussels' offer.

modules.i: Coercive economic measures are now a routine instrument of regional policy.
r: Hufbauer et al., Economic Sanctions Reconsidered, ch. 1
Course notes on the 2014 and 2022 measures
modules.a: Design a sanctions package for a hypothetical case, stating target, measure and success indicator.
modules.l: Sanctions rarely compel by pain alone; they change behaviour when they alter the target's calculation of costs against achievable concessions. Broad measures on whole economies tend to harden resistance, while targeted measures work through elite coalitions.

modules.i: The module turns the course material into an original country or thematic study.
modules.a: Submit a one-page proposal with question, case and sources.
modules.l: Regional research is source-hungry: official statistics, treaty texts and legal databases carry more weight than commentary. A narrow, well-documented case is stronger than a broad survey resting on secondary summaries.

courses.title: International Economics: Trade and Welfare
courses.description: Core international trade economics: the sources of gains from trade, the political economy of trade policy, and how tariffs, quotas and agreements redistribute welfare within and between countries.
objectives: Derive gains from trade using comparative advantage
Analyse tariff effects on consumers, producers and revenue
Evaluate non-tariff barriers and regional agreements
Interpret trade data and policy documents critically

modules.i: Why countries trade at all, and what determines the pattern of exchange.
r: Krugman, Obstfeld and Melitz, International Economics, ch. 2
Worked example sheet: two-country, two-good model
modules.a: Complete the two-country opportunity cost exercise and state the terms of trade range.
modules.l: Comparative advantage is about relative rather than absolute efficiency. A country gains from trade by specialising where its opportunity cost is lower, even if it is worse at everything in absolute terms, because the alternative is producing at home at a higher real cost.

modules.i: The Heckscher-Ohlin framework links trade patterns to relative factor abundance.
r: Reading summary: evidence on H-O predictions
modules.a: Apply the Stolper-Samuelson logic to a tariff on a labour-intensive good.
modules.l: Heckscher-Ohlin predicts that countries export goods intensive in their abundant factor. The Stolper-Samuelson theorem then explains why trade liberalisation creates domestic winners and losers: returns to the abundant factor rise while returns to the scarce factor fall.

modules.t: Economies of Scale and Intra-Industry Trade
modules.i: Much trade is between similar countries in similar goods, which endowment models cannot explain.
o: Distinguish internal from external scale economies
r: Case note: the European car market
modules.a: Classify ten trade flows as inter- or intra-industry and explain the pattern.
modules.l: Scale economies make specialisation self-reinforcing and generate two-way trade in differentiated products. The gains then come from variety and lower average cost rather than from exploiting factor differences, which changes what liberalisation is expected to deliver.

modules.i: A tariff is a tax on imports whose incidence can be decomposed precisely.
r: Problem set: partial equilibrium tariff model
modules.a: Calculate the welfare effects of a 15 percent tariff using the supplied supply and demand schedule.
modules.l: In partial equilibrium a tariff transfers surplus to producers, extracts revenue, and destroys surplus in two triangles. For a large country a terms-of-trade gain may offset part of the loss, but that gain is paid for by trading partners, which invites retaliation.

modules.i: Standards, quotas and administrative costs now bind trade more tightly than tariffs.
r: WTO World Trade Report (chapter on NTMs)
modules.a: Evaluate three product standards as trade barriers, distinguishing protection from legitimate regulation.
modules.l: The central difficulty with non-tariff measures is that the same instrument can serve public safety and domestic producers. Analysts therefore look for evidence of discrimination and for the availability of less restrictive alternatives.

modules.i: Preferential agreements liberalise inside the bloc while discriminating outside it.
o: Apply the GATT Article XXIV test
r: Course note: rules of origin in practice
modules.a: Assess whether a proposed customs union creates or diverts trade, with numbers.
modules.l: Viner's distinction remains the analytical core: an agreement raises welfare when trade creation dominates diversion. Deep agreements add regulatory harmonisation, whose gains are larger but whose distribution is harder to measure.

modules.i: Whether openness causes growth is one of the most contested questions in the field.
r: Rodrik, 'The Global Governance of Trade as if Development Really Mattered'
World Bank case note on value-chain upgrading
modules.a: Argue for or against infant-industry protection using one historical case.
modules.l: Cross-country correlations between openness and growth are hard to interpret because policy is not randomly assigned. Value-chain data sharpens the question, showing that what a country does within a chain matters more than how much it trades.

modules.i: Students apply the toolkit to a live trade policy proposal.
modules.a: Submit the policy brief analysing a proposed safeguard measure.
modules.l: A sound trade policy memo separates efficiency from distribution: total welfare may rise while identifiable groups lose. Naming the losers, their size and the feasible compensation is what distinguishes analysis from advocacy.

courses.title: Monetary Policy and Global Capital Flows
courses.description: Open-economy macroeconomics: exchange-rate regimes, interest parity, central bank credibility, sudden stops and the policy trilemma, applied to emerging-market crises.
objectives: Read a balance of payments and interpret its components
Apply interest parity conditions to exchange-rate expectations
Analyse currency crises with first- and second-generation models
Evaluate policy options under the trilemma

modules.i: The accounting identity that organises all open-economy analysis.
o: Explain the identity in accounting terms
r: IMF Balance of Payments Manual, overview chapter
modules.a: Decompose one country's balance of payments and explain the financing side.
modules.l: A current-account deficit is matched by net capital inflow by construction, so its meaning depends on what the inflow finances. Deficits driven by investment differ fundamentally from deficits driven by consumption, which is why the identity alone never settles the policy question.

modules.i: From hard pegs to floats, the regime determines which shocks a country absorbs.
r: IMF Annual Report on Exchange Arrangements, introduction
modules.a: Rank five regimes by their exposure to a terms-of-trade shock and justify the ranking.
modules.l: A peg imports monetary policy and exports adjustment to domestic wages and prices. Floating restores monetary autonomy but transmits external shocks through the currency, so the choice is about which adjustment is politically and economically cheaper.

modules.i: Covered and uncovered parity connect interest differentials to expected depreciation.
modules.a: Compute the forward rate implied by parity and compare it with the quoted market rate.
modules.l: Covered parity is an arbitrage condition that holds closely; uncovered parity is a behavioural claim that fails in the data. The failure is itself informative, because it prices risk and makes the carry trade profitable on average and catastrophic occasionally.

modules.i: Inflation outcomes depend on expectations, which depend on institutions.
r: Kydland and Prescott, 'Rules Rather than Discretion'
Course note on inflation targeting in emerging markets
modules.a: Analyse a disinflation episode and identify the evidence for anchored expectations.
modules.l: If policy is discretionary, the temptation to inflate after wages are set produces an inflationary bias with no output gain. Delegation to an independent central bank with a clear mandate is a commitment device, and its value shows up in the output cost of disinflation.

modules.i: Fixed rates, free capital movement and monetary autonomy cannot all hold.
r: IMF institutional view on capital flows
modules.a: Choose a corner of the trilemma for a small open economy and defend it.
modules.l: The trilemma is a constraint, not a recommendation: every regime sacrifices one objective. Capital-flow management has moved from taboo to toolkit, but measures must be temporary and targeted to avoid substituting for necessary adjustment.

modules.i: Crises combine weak fundamentals with self-fulfilling expectations.
modules.a: Reconstruct a crisis timeline and mark where fundamentals and expectations each dominated.
modules.l: First-generation models predict collapse when reserves run out under a financed deficit; second-generation models show that a peg can break because investors expect it to break. Most real crises contain both mechanisms, which is why diagnosis precedes prescription.

modules.i: Policy rates reach the economy through credit, asset prices and the exchange rate.
r: Course reader: transmission in emerging markets
BIS paper on global financial conditions
modules.a: Model the transmission of a rate rise in a highly dollarised economy and explain the weakened channel.
modules.l: Where liabilities are dollar-denominated and revenues are not, depreciation tightens balance sheets instead of stimulating net exports. Transmission then runs through credit risk, and the exchange rate becomes a financial-stability variable rather than a competitiveness one.

modules.i: Students run a small open-economy model under alternative shocks and regimes.
modules.a: Run the three assigned scenarios and submit the comparison memo.
modules.l: Simulations discipline intuition: the same shock produces very different paths under a peg and a float. The exercise is not forecasting but structured comparison, and the memo is graded on identifying which parameter drives the divergence.

courses.title: Comparative Politics: Institutions and Regimes
courses.description: How constitutions, electoral systems, executives and courts shape who governs and how power is constrained, compared across democracies and authoritarian regimes.
objectives: Classify regimes using explicit criteria
Explain how electoral rules shape party systems
Compare presidential and parliamentary government
Assess judicial independence comparatively

modules.i: The field's object is variation: why similar societies produce different regimes.
r: Lijphart, 'Comparative Politics and the Comparative Method'
modules.a: Take one concept and show where it stretches across two cases.
modules.l: Comparison is the substitute for experiment: with few cases and no control, the analyst must choose cases to make rival explanations distinguishable. Much of the field's rigour comes from saying explicitly what a case can and cannot prove.

modules.i: Regime classification is theory-laden and consequential.
o: Apply minimal and maximal definitions of democracy
r: Levitsky and Way, Competitive Authoritarianism, ch. 1
modules.a: Classify three regimes with a scoring rubric and defend the borderline call.
modules.l: Minimal definitions focus on contestation and participation, which makes them measurable; maximal definitions include outcomes, which makes them normatively richer but analytically slippery. Hybrid-regime concepts exist because many cases satisfy the form of democracy without its substance.

modules.i: The separation or fusion of powers structures accountability.
modules.a: Argue whether presidentialism is riskier for democratic survival, using two cases.
modules.l: Linz's claim that presidentialism is fragile rests on dual legitimacy and fixed terms; critics answer that survival depends on party systems and constitutional detail rather than the executive form alone. The comparison is a lesson in how cases are selected.

modules.i: The rules of counting votes determine who is represented and how.
o: Explain Duverger's law and its limits
modules.a: Calculate a disproportionality index for two simulated elections.
modules.l: Electoral rules are the most manipulable institutions in a constitution. Because they convert votes into seats non-linearly, small changes can reshape party systems, which is why reform proposals are rarely technical.

modules.i: Territorial distribution of authority manages diversity and creates new veto players.
modules.a: Compare two federal systems on the allocation of taxing power.
modules.l: Federal arrangements buy accommodation at the price of coordination. Where regional governments control revenue or veto constitutional change, national policy becomes a negotiation, and the same structure that prevents secession can paralyse decision-making.

modules.i: Party systems aggregate interests and structure government formation.
r: Lipset and Rokkan, Party Systems and Voter Alignments, introduction
modules.a: Chart two party systems over three elections and describe the trend.
modules.l: A party system is more than a count of parties: institutionalisation captures whether labels, organisations and voter attachments are stable. Where it is low, coalitions are transactional and accountability is weak.

modules.t: Courts and the Rule of Law
modules.i: Judicial power depends on appointment, tenure and the willingness of others to comply.
r: Case note on a court crisis
modules.a: Analyse one judicial crisis and identify the point at which independence was lost.
modules.l: Courts cannot enforce their own rulings, so independence is ultimately political: it survives as long as competing actors find it useful. Reform of appointment and tenure is therefore the standard route to capture, and the standard indicator of backsliding.

modules.i: Why some regimes fall and others adapt to the same pressures.
r: O'Donnell and Schmitter, Transitions from Authoritarian Rule
Geddes, 'What Do We Know About Democratization After Twenty Years?'
modules.a: Compare two regimes facing similar protests and explain the divergent outcomes.
modules.l: Transitions depend on splits within the ruling coalition as much as on pressure from below. Regimes that manage elite cohesion and distribute rents adapt; those that fracture under protest collapse, which is why outcomes differ despite similar street politics.

courses.title: Political Behaviour and Public Opinion
courses.description: How citizens form political attitudes, how those attitudes are measured, and how survey and experimental evidence should be interpreted.
objectives: Design a survey instrument free of common biases
Explain socialisation and ideology formation
Evaluate media-effects evidence
Interpret experimental results critically

modules.i: Behavioural research depends on measurement, and measurement depends on theory.
modules.a: Critique the methodology section of a published poll on a political topic.
modules.l: Attitudes are inferred, never observed, so every survey statistic combines a real signal with question wording, mode and sample effects. Reading method appendices is what separates interpretation from recitation.

modules.i: Where political identities come from, and how durable they are.
o: Distinguish parental transmission from peer effects
r: Jennings and Niemi, The Political Character of Adolescence
modules.a: Design a cohort comparison that could test generational replacement.
modules.l: Most political identities form early and persist, which makes generational replacement a powerful engine of slow change. But persistence is conditional: critical events can re-anchor a cohort's politics for decades.

modules.i: Do voters hold coherent ideologies or narrow issue positions?
r: Converse, 'The Nature of Belief Systems in Mass Publics'
Feldman, 'Structure and Consistency in Public Opinion'
modules.a: Test ideological consistency in a small dataset and report the pattern.
modules.l: Converse found that mass belief systems are loosely constrained compared with elite ones. Later research shows constraint rising with political engagement, which reframes the question as one about attention rather than capacity.

modules.i: Small wording choices produce large differences in measured opinion.
r: Krosnick and Presser, 'Question and Questionnaire Design'
modules.a: Rewrite three flawed survey items and explain each correction.
modules.l: Respondents answer the question they hear, not the one intended. Double-barrelled items, missing middle options and leading premises each shift results measurably, so pre-testing is a validity requirement rather than a polish.

modules.i: Party identification is the strongest single predictor of the vote.
o: Assess issue voting and economic voting
r: Campbell et al., The American Voter, ch. 6
modules.a: Model vote choice with party ID and economic evaluations and compare coefficients.
modules.l: Partisanship works as a perceptual filter: it shapes what voters see before it shapes what they choose. That is why economic voting is real but usually conditional on who is held responsible.

modules.i: What media do to attitudes, and what citizens actually encounter.
r: Iyengar and Kinder, News That Matters
modules.a: Compare two framings of one policy and predict the attitudinal difference.
modules.l: Effects are strongest on what people consider important and weakest on what they conclude. Selective exposure then limits even that: audiences self-sort into information environments that reinforce prior beliefs.

modules.i: Demand-side explanations for the populist surge and affective polarisation.
r: Course note on affective polarisation measures
modules.a: Test two explanations for populist support against available survey items.
modules.l: Populism is a thin ideology dividing society into a virtuous people and a corrupt elite; polarisation is an emotional distance between partisan camps. They correlate but are distinct, and conflating them misdiagnoses both.

modules.i: Randomisation buys causal identification at the cost of external validity.
o: Interpret treatment effects and confidence intervals
r: Druckman et al., Cambridge Handbook of Experimental Political Science, ch. 1
modules.a: Write a pre-analysis plan for a survey experiment on a course topic.
modules.l: An experiment identifies the effect of a manipulation in a specific setting with a specific sample. The inference to a general claim is an argument, not a result, which is why replication and pre-registration carry so much weight.

courses.title: Public International Law
courses.description: The sources, subjects and mechanisms of international law: treaties, custom, state responsibility, jurisdiction and the peaceful settlement of disputes.
objectives: Identify and apply the sources of international law
Interpret treaty provisions using the Vienna Convention
Apply the rules of state responsibility
Analyse international disputes using case law

modules.i: Article 38 of the ICJ Statute organises the materials of legal argument.
modules.a: Argue whether a stated practice has crystallised into custom, citing evidence of both elements.
modules.l: Custom requires both a general practice and opinio juris, though the second element is inferred from conduct. The argumentative work lies in establishing that the practice is sufficiently widespread and that it was followed out of legal obligation.

modules.i: The Vienna Convention supplies the grammar of treaty law.
o: Apply the rules on conclusion and entry into force
r: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Articles 19-33
modules.a: Interpret a disputed clause using the Article 31 method and record each step.
modules.l: Article 31 places text, context and purpose in a single interpretative operation, with preparatory work only supplementary. Reservations are permitted unless they defeat the object and purpose, a test that has generated most of the practical friction.

modules.i: Who can hold rights and duties under international law, and in what measure.
r: Reparation for Injuries, ICJ Advisory Opinion
modules.a: Apply the statehood criteria to an unrecognised entity and defend the conclusion.
modules.l: Statehood rests on factual criteria, while recognition is declaratory in doctrine and constitutive in practice. The gap between the two is where much political conflict is fought in legal form.

modules.i: Which state may prescribe and enforce law, and which officials are shielded.
modules.a: Analyse a cross-border criminal case for competing jurisdictional claims.
modules.l: Jurisdiction is primarily territorial, with narrow extra-territorial extensions. Immunities do not deny the wrongfulness of conduct; they bar proceedings in foreign courts, which is why accountability often depends on waiver or on international tribunals.

modules.i: When a breach engages responsibility, and what follows from it.
r: ILC Articles on State Responsibility, Articles 1-31
modules.a: Determine responsibility for conduct by a non-state group and state your reasoning.
modules.l: Responsibility requires conduct attributable to a state and inconsistent with its obligation. Attribution is the hard element in practice, particularly where private actors operate with tacit state support.

modules.i: The prohibition and its exceptions define the legal boundary of war.
r: Nicaragua v United States, ICJ 1986, paras 187-201
modules.a: Assess a claimed self-defence action against the Caroline criteria.
modules.l: Self-defence requires an armed attack, necessity and proportionality. Controversy concentrates on whether an attack must have occurred, and on the evidential standard for pre-emptive claims, which state practice has not settled.

modules.i: Negotiation, arbitration and adjudication each carry different costs.
o: Explain consent as the basis of jurisdiction
r: Course note on ICJ jurisdiction clauses
modules.a: Evaluate whether an ICJ case is admissible given the parties' declarations.
modules.l: International adjudication is consensual, so jurisdiction is routinely contested before the merits. Provisional measures bind in principle, but enforcement depends on the Security Council and on the parties' reputational stakes.

modules.t: Case Study: A Dispute Before the Court
modules.i: Students brief and argue a composite dispute in a moot setting.
o: Brief a case from pleadings to judgment
Construct a legal argument from sources
r: Selected case pleadings in the course pack
modules.a: Submit the applicant's memorial and take part in the moot hearing.
modules.l: A memorial succeeds by building a chain from source to conclusion without gaps: jurisdiction, applicable law, breach, and remedy. Each link is a distinct argument and examiners grade the chain, not the rhetoric.

courses.title: International Humanitarian Law
courses.description: The law governing armed conflict: distinction, proportionality, protected persons, occupation, and individual accountability for war crimes.
objectives: Apply the principles of distinction and proportionality
Identify protected persons and objects
Analyse occupation law questions
Assess individual criminal responsibility frameworks

modules.i: Humanitarian law grew from battlefield custom into a treaty regime.
o: Trace the Geneva and Hague traditions
r: Course note on IHL's historical development
modules.a: Classify three conflicts as international or non-international, with reasons.
modules.l: IHL applies when armed conflict exists, whatever the legality of its initiation. The classification matters because the applicable treaty rules differ, and because many contemporary conflicts mix both categories.

modules.i: The two principles that organise targeting law.
modules.a: Apply the proportionality test to a supplied targeting scenario and state the conclusion.
modules.l: Proportionality is not a balance of numbers but a prohibition on attacks expected to cause excessive incidental harm relative to military advantage. The analysis is ex ante, which is why evidence of what was known at the time matters.

modules.i: Civilians, prisoners, the wounded and medical facilities enjoy specific protections.
r: Course note on the wounded and sick
modules.a: Determine the status of three captured combatants under GC III.
modules.l: Status determines protection: lawful combatants captured become prisoners of war, while those who take direct part in hostilities without the privilege lose protection from attack but retain fundamental guarantees.

modules.i: Weapons and tactics are constrained independently of targeting.
o: Assess new technology within existing rules
r: Course note on autonomous weapons debates
modules.a: Evaluate whether a described tactic is perfidy or a lawful ruse.
modules.l: Perfidy invites the enemy's confidence and then betrays it, which endangers lawful practice; ruses mislead without breaching a protection. The distinction turns on whether a protected signal was abused.

modules.i: Effective control triggers a distinct set of obligations.
modules.a: Analyse a measure taken by an occupier against the applicable rules.
modules.l: Occupation law balances the occupier's security needs with the preservation of local institutions. Legislative change is permitted only within narrow limits, because the regime presumes temporary control rather than sovereignty.

modules.i: Individual responsibility operates through courts with limited reach.
modules.a: Draft the charge analysis for one scenario with the elements listed.
modules.l: War crimes require a serious violation in an armed conflict with a nexus to it. Command responsibility is a separate mode of liability resting on failure to prevent or punish, not on ordering.

modules.i: Two bodies of law overlap in armed conflict, sometimes awkwardly.
o: Explain the relationship between the regimes
r: Course note on detention and human rights
modules.a: Analyse a detention scenario under both regimes and reconcile the answers.
modules.l: Human rights law continues in armed conflict, with IHL the more specific rule on conduct of hostilities. Detention is the clearest case where the two regimes diverge and where the choice of framework determines legality.

modules.i: Students apply the full framework to a documented contemporary conflict.
modules.a: Submit the legal memorandum on two contested incidents.
modules.l: Legal qualification depends on verified facts: who was targeted, what was known, and what alternatives existed. A memorandum that asserts facts it cannot source earns no credit, however sound its law.

courses.title: The World in the Twentieth Century
courses.description: A global history of the twentieth century from the collapse of the old empires to the end of the Cold War, with attention to how war, ideology and decolonisation reshaped the international order.
objectives: Explain the causes and consequences of the two world wars
Analyse decolonisation as a global process
Trace the Cold War's phases and turning points
Read primary documents critically

modules.i: Industrial power, imperial rivalry and a fragile balance produced a volatile order.
modules.a: Draw the alliance map for 1914 and annotate two flashpoints.
modules.l: The pre-war order was not doomed by structure alone: decisions taken in July 1914 turned a regional crisis into a continental war. Contingency and rigidity interacted, which is why historians still disagree on responsibility.

modules.t: The Great War and the Versailles Settlement
modules.i: Total war transformed states, societies and the terms of peace.
modules.a: Evaluate whether the settlement could have been sustained, using two contemporary assessments.
modules.l: Versailles combined liberal rhetoric with punitive terms, and its enforcement depended on powers that later disengaged. The result was a settlement that neither reconciled Germany nor deterred it.

modules.i: Economic collapse, ideological conflict and weak institutions fed each other.
o: Assess the League of Nations' failures
r: Tooze, The Wages of Destruction, ch. 1
Primary document: League response to Manchuria
modules.a: Assess the Manchurian crisis as a test of collective security.
modules.l: The League failed less from absent law than from absent enforcement: great powers would not bear the cost of sanctions. The Depression then removed the economic margin that might have made cooperation survivable.

modules.i: A war of ideology and industrial mobilisation with a global reach.
o: Explain the war's expansion into a world conflict
modules.a: Compare two occupation regimes and their consequences for civilians.
modules.l: The war's course was decided by industrial capacity and by the coalition that pooled it. Occupation policy varied sharply, but in the east it was explicitly exterminatory, which places the war's violence at the centre of its history.

modules.i: Allied victory gave way to a divided Europe and a global contest.
o: Compare explanations of the Cold War's origins
modules.a: Argue for one explanation of the Cold War's origins and against another.
modules.l: Responsibility is distributed differently depending on whether one emphasises security needs, ideology or domestic politics. What is not disputed is that 1947 marked the point where ambiguity hardened into blocs.

modules.i: Empire dissolved through negotiation and war, reshaping the international system.
r: Darwin, The End of the British Empire, ch. 6
modules.a: Compare two independence processes on timing, violence and outcome.
modules.l: Decolonisation was driven by metropolitan weakness, organised nationalism and international pressure, but the mix varied. New states then entered a system whose rules and institutions they had not designed.

modules.i: Superpower accommodation coexisted with proxy conflict.
r: Gaddis, The Cold War: A New History, ch. 6
Primary document: Helsinki Final Act excerpt
modules.a: Assess whether détente stabilised the superpower relationship, with two pieces of evidence.
modules.l: Détente managed the nuclear competition without resolving the political contest, so it produced agreements and interventions simultaneously. Its collapse showed that arms control cannot carry a rivalry on its own.

modules.i: The end of the Cold War opened a brief unipolar moment.
o: Explain the collapse of the Eastern bloc
Analyse the post-Cold War order's assumptions
modules.a: Evaluate the claim that 1989 marked the end of the European order established in 1945.
modules.l: The 1989 revolutions were largely peaceful because elites declined to use force, which made the outcome depend on decisions rather than structures. The order that followed rested on assumptions about convergence that later decades tested severely.

courses.title: Empires, Trade and the Making of the Global Economy
courses.description: The economic history of empire from 1500 to 1900, tracing how coercion, finance and industrial production produced an integrated but deeply unequal world economy.
objectives: Explain the relationship between empire and trade
Analyse the Atlantic economy and coerced labour
Trace the gold standard's political foundations
Assess the legacies of imperial economic structures

modules.i: Long-distance trade knitted distant societies into new commodity chains.
r: Tracy, The Political Economy of Merchant Empires, ch. 1
Course map: Indian Ocean trade circa 1600
modules.a: Trace one commodity from source to market and identify each actor's margin.
modules.l: Early modern globalisation was built by chartered companies operating under state licence. Their profits depended less on free exchange than on the legal privileges, forts and shipping monopolies granted by European crowns.

modules.t: The Atlantic Economy and Coerced Labour
modules.i: Plantation slavery was an economic system, not an aberration.
o: Assess slavery's contribution to industrial capital
r: Eltis and Engerman, 'The Importance of Slavery in the Industrialization of the British Economy'
modules.a: Interpret the supplied voyage data and describe two patterns it establishes.
modules.l: Slavery was integral to Atlantic commerce: capital, shipping and insurance all adapted to it. Debates over its contribution to industrialisation turn on measurement, but not on whether the institution was economically central.

modules.i: Empires tried to capture trade surplus through navigation laws and monopolies.
r: McCusker and Menard, The Economy of British America, ch. 2
modules.a: Assess the costs and benefits of imperial regulation for colonial producers.
modules.l: Mercantilism sought a favourable balance through regulated trade, but enforcement was expensive and generated evasion. The political cost of regulation, rather than its economic burden, is what proved decisive in the American case.

modules.t: Industry, Railways and the New Trade
modules.i: Industrial production and transport changed the scale of exchange.
o: Assess the railway's impact on interior economies
r: O'Rourke and Williamson, Globalization and History, ch. 3
Course note on the transport revolution
modules.a: Compare freight cost data across two decades and explain the trade effect.
modules.l: Falling transport costs made bulk trade viable, converting distant interiors into commodity suppliers. That integration raised incomes but narrowed specialisation, leaving many economies exposed to single-commodity price swings.

modules.i: Colonial states built legal and fiscal systems that outlasted them.
r: Course note on colonial land registers
modules.a: Compare two administrative models on their fiscal and legal consequences.
modules.l: Colonial administration varied between assimilation and delegated authority, but both relied on codified custom and land registration. Those instruments reshaped property relations in ways that persisted after independence.

modules.i: Trade expansion sometimes required military force rather than settlement.
r: Primary document: Treaty of Nanjing extract
modules.a: Evaluate whether the opening of China was trade-driven or coercion-driven.
modules.l: Informal empire relied on treaty privileges, extraterritoriality and naval threat rather than annexation. It delivered market access at low administrative cost, and it entrenched the coercive character of nineteenth-century globalisation.

modules.t: Finance and the Classical Gold Standard
modules.i: Monetary arrangements were political achievements with distributional consequences.
modules.a: Analyse how a periphery country adjusted to a balance-of-payments deficit under gold.
modules.l: The gold standard coordinated exchange rates but pushed adjustment onto wages and employment. Creditor countries could sterilise inflows, while debtors had to deflate, which made the system politically fragile from the start.

modules.i: Students assess how imperial structures shaped later development.
r: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson, 'The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development'
Course reader: critique of the AJR thesis
modules.a: Defend or challenge the colonial-origins thesis using one regional case.
modules.l: Legacy arguments are powerful but must specify a mechanism: institutions, infrastructure, borders or human capital. Without that specification, correlation between colonial experience and contemporary outcomes explains little.

courses.title: Diplomatic Practice and Negotiation
courses.description: The craft of diplomacy: how missions work, how negotiators build and close agreements, and how protocol and communication shape outcomes.
objectives: Describe the structure and functions of diplomatic missions
Apply negotiation frameworks to bilateral cases
Draft diplomatic correspondence correctly
Conduct a structured negotiation simulation

modules.i: Diplomacy is the management of relations by communication rather than force.
r: Berridge, Diplomacy: Theory and Practice, ch. 1
Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, Articles 1-3
modules.a: Map the functions of a mission onto three real tasks and note where they conflict.
modules.l: Diplomacy substitutes continuous communication for episodic confrontation. Its value lies in the routine channels it provides, which allow states to clarify intentions before positions harden.

modules.i: Institutional design shapes what a state can know and do abroad.
modules.a: Draft a reporting cable on a supplied event, respecting clearance rules.
modules.l: A mission's influence depends on the quality and speed of its reporting. Coordination failures usually occur between ministries rather than within them, which is why clearances lengthen exactly when speed matters most.

modules.i: Notes, aides-mémoire and démarches have conventions that carry meaning.
r: Course pack: specimen notes with commentary
modules.a: Draft a note verbale protesting a consular decision.
modules.l: The form of a communication is itself a signal: a note verbale in the third person is routine, while a démarche delivered in person escalates. Choosing the channel is therefore part of the message.

modules.i: Interests, options and alternatives explain more than bargaining style.
r: Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes, ch. 2-3
modules.a: Separate stated positions from interests in a supplied brief and identify the ZOPA.
modules.l: Positions are what parties say they want; interests are why. Because the zone of possible agreement is defined by reservation points rather than by opening demands, the analyst's first task is estimating each side's alternative.

modules.i: Coalitions, sequencing and chairing decide outcomes in multilateral settings.
r: Zartman, 'The Political Economy of Multilateral Negotiation'
modules.a: Design a sequencing plan for a twelve-party negotiation on one issue.
modules.l: In multi-party talks the chair controls the agenda, and the agenda controls the outcome. A single negotiating text is a tool for forcing convergence: it converts bilateral objections into amendments everyone can see.

modules.i: Third parties change the game when they control information or resources.
r: Crocker, Hampson and Aall, Taming Intractable Conflicts, ch. 4
modules.a: Assess whether a described conflict is ripe for mediation, with reasoning.
modules.l: Mediation works when parties face a mutually hurting stalemate and a way out is visible. A mediator with no leverage can still help by clarifying interests, but cannot create the willingness that a stalemate produces.

modules.i: Order and ceremony encode political rank and recognition.
r: Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, Articles 4-14
modules.a: Resolve a precedence dispute between two delegations using the applicable rule.
modules.l: Protocol is not decoration: recognition, seniority and seating carry political meaning. Disputes over order are usually disputes about status, which is why they escalate far beyond their apparent importance.

modules.i: Students negotiate a bilateral agreement under time pressure.
o: Conduct a negotiation to a written outcome
r: Simulation pack: mandate, facts and roles
modules.a: Negotiate and submit the joint text plus a personal debrief.
modules.l: Preparation determines the outcome: the side that knows its own reservation point and the other side's constraints controls the pace. The debrief matters as much as the agreement, because it names the reasoning behind each concession.
